endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Implement reasonable measures to prevent, flag, or take other action in response to outputs that reproduce particular training data (e.g., plagiarized, trademarked, patented, licensed content or trade secret material).

endorsements.title: Advancing the diagnosis of major depressive disorder: Integrating neuroimaging and machine learning
endorsements.quote: However, for more complex models, such as DL, their inherent complexity often requires post-hoc explainability techniques, such as local interpretable model-agnostic explanations and SHAP, to improve the oversight of decision-making processes[ 78 , 79 ].

endorsements.title: Ethical framework for responsible foundational models in medical imaging
endorsements.quote: The inherent opacity of these sophisticated models, often characterized as “blackbox”, necessitates advanced explainable AI techniques to establish trust among healthcare providers and patients alike.

endorsements.title: Current status and future directions of AI in prostate cancer detection on MRI: a special report from the ESUR prostate MRI working group authors
endorsements.quote: Manufacturers should promote transparency and explainability in how the AI system works, often through techniques like speciali zed visualizations to help users understand the model \u2019s decisions and limitations, thereby fostering trust.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether counterfactual prompts, attribution analysis, or other explainability techniques make generative AI outputs in health care traceable or understandable. The recommendation rests on one federal framework and two commentaries, and none of them reports outcome data.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are a framework and two commentaries. The commentaries concern imaging and depression diagnosis models, where SHAP and LIME apply to predictive rather than generative systems, which may limit how directly they bear on generative outputs.

The NIST Generative AI Profile uses should-level language, but its quoted text asks deployers to flag outputs that reproduce training data such as licensed or trademarked content. That provision addresses provenance and intellectual property more than clinical explainability, so it offers partial support for attribution methods and does not by itself establish an explainability requirement.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that apply counterfactual prompting or attribution analysis to generative models used in clinical settings and measure whether clinicians detect erroneous outputs more often, whether explanations are faithful to model behavior, and what time burden the techniques add to review. No supplied study addresses any of these outcomes.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no data on whether explanations produced by these techniques would be understandable or useful to their clinicians or patients.
